title: [Full Workshop] Building Metrics that actually work — David Karam, Pi Labs (fmr Google Search)
talk_summary: A Pi Labs workshop arguing that evals should be a layered 'scoring system' of many cheap, objective signals (like Google's ~300 search signals) rather than a single LLM-judge prompt, calibrated against real human labels via confusion matrices. They demo a copilot that decomposes a subjective criterion into weighted dimensions, then use that scorer for model comparison, prompt regression testing, and best-of-N sampling at inference time.

takeaways.technique: Decompose one subjective gate into many weighted objective signals
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of asking an LLM 'is this helpful?', they break the judgment into many small inspectable questions/code checks, each weighted critical/major/minor, and combine them into one score.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if instead you just go and say, "Hey, is this a helpful response?" Mostly what you're doing is delegating that that eval to the LLM itself

takeaways.technique: Calibrate scorer against labeled outcomes with a confusion matrix
takeaways.what_they_do: They run the scoring system over a labeled dataset (thumbs up/down) and inspect a confusion matrix of agreement, iterating dimensions until alignment improves.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Metrics that work are not necessarily good metrics or bad metrics. They're either calibrated metrics or unccalibrated metrics.
takeaways.numbers: ~120 labeled examples in the spreadsheet exercise

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate several responses at higher temperature, score each with the cheap scorer, and return the best one — described as online reinforcement learning without changing prompts or models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: generate four or five responses and then score those responses online and see which one's the best one and you get a pretty decent lift
takeaways.numbers: score steadily going up as number of samples increases

takeaways.technique: Use the scorer to compare models and prompts on a fixed eval set
takeaways.what_they_do: They run the same ~10 examples through multiple models and prompt variants and compare scores to detect regressions before shipping a change.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can eva use your scoring system for evaluating different models

takeaways.technique: Start with a handful of correlated signals, grow incrementally
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than building a comprehensive metric suite upfront, start with 5-10 simple signals known to correlate with goodness, then add dimensions as bugs surface.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Maybe you start with five, 10 signals that you know for a fact are correlated with goodness.

takeaways.technique: Low-variance scorer models instead of generative judges
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue decoder LLMs are creative and post-hoc justify scores; a regression-head scorer gives near-identical scores on repeat runs, enabling cheap online scoring.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you run the same score twice on the same thing it's not going to give you different scores
